claim: In prostate cancer, resistance to the antiandrogen enzalutamide (Enz) can occur through bypass of androgen receptor (AR) blockade by the glucocorticoid receptor (GR).
source: In prostate cancer, resistance to the antiandrogen enzalutamide (Enz) can occur through bypass of androgen receptor (AR) blockade by the glucocorticoid receptor (GR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: GR-mediated antiandrogen resistance is adaptive and reversible due to regulation of GR expression by a tissue-specific enhancer.
source: In contrast to fixed genomic alterations, here we show that GR-mediated antiandrogen resistance is adaptive and reversible due to regulation of GR expression by a tissue-specific enhancer.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing dynamic GR expression changes with Enz exposure.

claim: GR expression is silenced in prostate cancer by a combination of AR binding and EZH2-mediated repression at the GR locus.
source: GR expression is silenced in prostate cancer by a combination of AR binding and EZH2-mediated repression at the GR locus, but is restored in advanced prostate cancers upon reversion of both repressive signals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data showing AR binding and H3K27me3 marks at the GR locus.

claim: GR expression is restored in advanced prostate cancers upon reversion of both repressive signals (AR binding and EZH2-mediated repression).
source: GR expression is silenced in prostate cancer by a combination of AR binding and EZH2-mediated repression at the GR locus, but is restored in advanced prostate cancers upon reversion of both repressive signals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing increased GR expression in post-Enz/Abi CRPC samples.

claim: BET bromodomain inhibition resensitizes drug-resistant tumors to Enz by selectively impairing the GR signaling axis via the GR enhancer.
source: Remarkably, BET bromodomain inhibition resensitizes drug-resistant tumors to Enz by selectively impairing the GR signaling axis via this enhancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo xenograft experiments showing tumor regression with JQ1+Enz combination treatment.

claim: Overall survival of CRPC patients is significantly improved by treatment with next generation AR pathway inhibitors such as abiraterone (Abi) and enzalutamide (Enz).
source: Overall survival of CRPC patients is significantly improved by treatment with next generation AR pathway inhibitors such as abiraterone (Abi) and enzalutamide (Enz) that more effectively target the AR signaling axis (Scher et al., 2012; de Bono et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published clinical studies.

claim: Acquired resistance to AR pathway inhibitors is a major clinical problem.
source: However, acquired resistance to these drugs is a major clinical problem.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: A common mechanism of acquired resistance to all targeted therapies is genetic mutation.
source: A common mechanism of acquired resistance to all targeted therapies is genetic mutation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to examples in kinase inhibitors and nuclear receptor antagonists.

claim: AR mutations or gene amplifications can confer resistance to antiandrogen therapy in prostate cancer, including Enz.
source: For example, AR mutations or gene amplifications can confer resistance to antiandrogen therapy in prostate cancer, including Enz (Balbas et al., 2013; Joseph et al., 2013; Watson et al., 2015), and estrogen receptor (ER) mutations confer resistance to ER pathway therapies in breast cancer (Robinson et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Estrogen receptor (ER) mutations confer resistance to ER pathway therapies in breast cancer.
source: For example, AR mutations or gene amplifications can confer resistance to antiandrogen therapy in prostate cancer, including Enz (Balbas et al., 2013; Joseph et al., 2013; Watson et al., 2015), and estrogen receptor (ER) mutations confer resistance to ER pathway therapies in breast cancer (Robinson et al., 2013; Toy et al., 2013; Jeselsohn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: BRAF mutant colorectal cancers are resistant to kinase inhibition due to activation of EGFR caused by a BRAF-dependent negative feedback loop.
source: BRAF mutant colorectal cancers are resistant to kinase inhibition due to activation of EGFR caused by a BRAF-dependent negative feedback loop (Prahallad et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Notch-mutant T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemias (T-ALL) treated with gamma-secretase inhibitors (GSIs) develop an epigenetic, reversible state and subsequent activation of downstream transcriptional programs that bypass the GSI blockade.
source: Similarly, Notch-mutant T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemias (T-ALL) treated with gamma-secretase inhibitors (GSIs) develop an epigenetic, reversible state and subsequent activation of downstream transcriptional programs that bypass the GSI blockade (Knoechel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: GR upregulation was found in 8 of 13 independent Enz-resistant tumor clones.
source: GR upregulation was found in 8 of 13 independent Enz-resistant tumor clones.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from the study.

claim: GR expression in LREX' cells was dynamic and could be toggled on and off based on Enz exposure, consistent with an AR-mediated negative feedback.
source: GR expression in LREX' cells was dynamic and could be toggled on and off based on Enz exposure, consistent with an AR-mediated negative feedback (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Enz treatment did not result in significant GR upregulation in Enz-sensitive LNAR' cells or in GR-negative resistant clones.
source: Conversely, Enz treatment did not result in significant GR upregulation in Enz-sensitive LNAR' cells or in GR-negative resistant clones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a second level of GR regulation beyond AR inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dexamethasone (Dex) treatment partially restored growth and rescued AR target gene expression in the presence of Enz in the CRPC organoid line (MSK-PCa2).
source: The importance of GR as a resistance mechanism was also evident in the CRPC organoid line (MSK-PCa2) (Gao et al., 2014), where dexamethasone (Dex) treatment partially restored growth and rescued AR target gene expression in the presence of Enz (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid growth assays and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Whole exome sequencing of LNAR' and LREX' cells did not reveal any gene-coding mutations associated with Enz resistance.
source: Whole exome sequencing of LNAR' and LREX' cells did not reveal any gene-coding mutations associated with Enz resistance; therefore, we considered epigenetic mechanisms.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from whole exome sequencing analysis.

claim: Previous studies of GR transcriptional regulation have largely focused on the proximal promoter, which is the primary mechanism of GR regulation in most tissue types.
source: Previous studies of GR transcriptional regulation have largely focused on the proximal promoter, which is the primary mechanism of GR regulation in most tissue types (Breslin et al., 2001; McGowan et al., 2009; Nobukuni et al., 1995; Nunez and Vedeckis, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ChIP-seq analysis identified a clear enhancer at the GR gene (NR3C1) locus in LNAR' and LREX' cells, regardless of Enz treatment.
source: This analysis identified a clear enhancer (revealed by the H3K4me1 track) (Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011; Creyghton et al., 2010) in LNAR' and LREX' cells, regardless of Enz treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The GR enhancer and promoter both had clearly defined active chromatin marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me3, respectively) in LREX' cells treated with Enz.
source: Consistent with the high level of GR mRNA expression in LREX' cells treated with Enz, this enhancer and the GR promoter both had clearly defined active chromatin marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me3, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The lack of active chromatin marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me3) in LNAR' cells signified a poised GR enhancer state.
source: Conversely, the lack of these active marks in LNAR' cells signified a poised GR enhancer state.
evidence: This claim is inferred from ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CRISPR-mediated deletion of the GR enhancer resulted in a 60 percent reduction in Enz-induced GR expression in LREX' cells.
source: LREX' cells lacking the enhancer showed a 60 percent reduction in Enz-induced GR expression as measured by quantitative PCR (qPCR) (Figure 1C), validating its importance in regulating GR transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ChromHMM analysis confirmed active promoters at the GR locus in most tissues, but minimal evidence of a GR enhancer.
source: This analysis confirmed active promoters at the GR locus in most tissues, but minimal evidence of a GR enhancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChromHMM analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Kidney and liver tissue (and HEPG2 liver cancer cells) show evidence of a weak or poised enhancer at the GR locus.
source: Exceptions include kidney and liver tissue (and HEPG2 liver cancer cells), with evidence of a weak or poised enhancer, and pancreas and gastric tissue with spotty chromatin marks in this region.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChromHMM analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A clearly defined enhancer (H3K4me1) was revealed in every prostate tissue examined, including normal and malignant samples.
source: In contrast to the non-prostate tissues, this analysis revealed a clearly defined enhancer (H3K4me1) in every prostate tissue examined, including in Enz-treated LREX' cells which also have the active H3K27ac enhancer mark (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChromHMM analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GR is robustly expressed in both basal and luminal cells in normal prostate tissue, but substantially reduced in primary prostate cancer.
source: GR is robustly expressed in both basal and luminal cells in normal prostate tissue, but substantially reduced in primary prostate cancer (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is a significant decrease in GR mRNA levels in primary prostate cancer relative to normal tissue.
source: Consistent with the IHC data, we observed a significant decrease in GR mRNA levels in primary prostate cancer relative to normal tissue, with a further decrease in CRPC samples from patients who have not received Enz or Abi (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by meta-analysis of RNA expression datasets shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a further decrease in GR mRNA levels in CRPC samples from patients who have not received Enz or Abi compared to primary prostate cancer.
source: Consistent with the IHC data, we observed a significant decrease in GR mRNA levels in primary prostate cancer relative to normal tissue, with a further decrease in CRPC samples from patients who have not received Enz or Abi (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by meta-analysis of RNA expression datasets shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mean GR mRNA levels were significantly increased in CRPC samples obtained after Enz/Abi treatment.
source: However, mean GR mRNA levels were significantly increased in CRPC samples obtained after Enz/Abi treatment but not back to the levels seen in primary disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by meta-analysis of RNA expression datasets shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The increase in mean GR level in post-Enz/Abi patients is explained, in part, by a subset of patients with higher GR expression.
source: More detailed analysis of the post-Enz/Abi patients revealed that the increase in mean GR level is explained, in part, by a subset of patients with higher GR expression, consistent with our previous finding of increased GR protein expression in a subset of Enz-treated patients (Arora et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA expression data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: There were no differences in tumor and stromal cell content in the CRPC pre- versus post-Enz/Abi samples.
source: We also performed computational analyses to compare tumor and stromal cell content and found no differences in the CRPC pre- versus post-Enz/Abi samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational tumor purity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AR binding peaks were detected at the GR enhancer in 5 of 5 primary prostate tumors, but not in the matched normal tissue.
source: Remarkably, AR binding peaks were detected at the GR enhancer in 5 of 5 tumors, but not in the matched normal tissue (Figure 2C), precisely correlating with reduced GR mRNA levels seen in primary cancers versus normal tissue (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: AR binding at the GR enhancer site is repressive.
source: We therefore postulate that AR binding at the GR enhancer site is repressive, as has been reported for an AR binding site within the AR genomic locus (Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a postulation based on data and supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The differential AR binding at the GR enhancer in normal versus cancer is consistent with extensive reprogramming of the AR cistrome reported in human prostate tumors.
source: The differential AR binding at this enhancer in normal versus cancer, despite comparable levels of AR expression, is consistent with extensive reprogramming of the AR cistrome reported in human prostate tumors (Pomerantz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data and a citation to a published study.

claim: Increased H3K27me3 was observed at the GR promoter and enhancer in cancer samples (MSK-PCa2, LNAR') compared to normal prostate cells.
source: We observed increased H3K27me3 at the GR promoter and enhancer in the cancer samples (MSK-PCa2, LNAR') compared to normal prostate cells, but loss of the H3K27me3 mark in Enz-resistant LREX' cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Loss of the H3K27me3 mark was observed at the GR promoter and enhancer in Enz-resistant LREX' cells.
source: We observed increased H3K27me3 at the GR promoter and enhancer in the cancer samples (MSK-PCa2, LNAR') compared to normal prostate cells, but loss of the H3K27me3 mark in Enz-resistant LREX' cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: H3K27me3 at the GR locus is correlated with reduced GR expression.
source: The results show that H3K27me3 at the GR locus is correlated with reduced expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between H3K27me3 levels and GR expression shown in the data.

claim: Treatment with GSK126 alone had no effect on GR levels in LNAR' cells.
source: Although treatment with GSK126 alone had no effect, GR levels rose more than 30-fold in combination with Enz, to levels comparable to those seen in LREX' cells treated with Enz alone (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: GR levels rose more than 30-fold in LNAR' cells treated with GSK126 in combination with Enz.
source: Although treatment with GSK126 alone had no effect, GR levels rose more than 30-fold in combination with Enz, to levels comparable to those seen in LREX' cells treated with Enz alone (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Similar cooperativity between GSK126 and Enz was observed in MSK-PCa2 tumor organoids but not in normal prostate organoids.
source: We observed similar cooperativity between GSK126 and Enz in MSK-PCa2 tumor organoids but not in normal prostate organoids that lack H3K27me3 or AR binding at the GR locus (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: GR expression in prostate tissue is silenced during the transition to cancer by a combination of AR binding and PRC2-mediated repression at the GR locus.
source: Together, these data suggest that GR expression in prostate tissue is silenced during the transition to cancer by a combination of AR binding and PRC2-mediated repression at the GR locus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: The PRC2 mark can be erased in late stage CRPC (post-Enz/Abi), which enables cells to express GR when exposed to Enz.
source: We postulate that the PRC2 mark can be erased in late stage CRPC (post-Enz/Abi), which enables cells to express GR when exposed to Enz, as Enz treatment displaces AR repression from the GR enhancer.
evidence: This is a postulation based on the experimental observations.

claim: In vitro treatment of LREX' cells with the BET inhibitor JQ1 resulted in a dose-dependent decrease of GR expression.
source: Indeed, in vitro treatment of LREX' cells with the BET inhibitor JQ1 (Filippakopoulos et al., 2010) resulted in a dose-dependent decrease of GR expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No changes in H3K27ac, H3K27me3 or H3K4me1 at the GR enhancer were observed with JQ1 treatment.
source: Consistent with BET bromodomains being epigenetic readers as opposed to writers or erasers, we observed no changes in H3K27ac, H3K27me3 or H3K4me1 at the GR enhancer with JQ1 treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BET inhibitors interfere with AR function by blocking recruitment of AR to chromatin and impairing expression of downstream target genes rather than directly lowering AR mRNA levels.
source: BET inhibitors are reported to interfere with AR function, but through a different mechanism, by blocking recruitment of AR to chromatin and impairing expression of downstream target genes rather than directly lowering AR mRNA levels (Asangani et al., 2014; Faivre et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2015); however, we did not observe effects of JQ1 on AR binding at the GR enhancer (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies and ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No effects of JQ1 on AR binding at the GR enhancer were observed.
source: BET inhibitors are reported to interfere with AR function, but through a different mechanism, by blocking recruitment of AR to chromatin and impairing expression of downstream target genes rather than directly lowering AR mRNA levels (Asangani et al., 2014; Faivre et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2015); however, we did not observe effects of JQ1 on AR binding at the GR enhancer (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LNAR' tumors showed no response to JQ1 treatment despite retaining their sensitivity to Enz.
source: Remarkably, LNAR' tumors showed no response to JQ1 treatment despite retaining their well-documented sensitivity to Enz and dependency on AR-signaling (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RNA-seq analysis of JQ1-treated LNAR' tumors confirmed that the canonical BET-dependent gene MYC was potently downregulated.
source: This is particularly striking because RNA-seq analysis of JQ1-treated LNAR' tumors confirmed that the canonical BET-dependent gene MYC was potently downregulated, thereby validating sufficient JQ1 exposure, with no changes in AR target genes such as NKX3.1 (Figure 3C) or an AR target gene signature, as discussed below (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No changes in AR target genes such as NKX3.1 were observed in JQ1-treated LNAR' tumors.
source: This is particularly striking because RNA-seq analysis of JQ1-treated LNAR' tumors confirmed that the canonical BET-dependent gene MYC was potently downregulated, thereby validating sufficient JQ1 exposure, with no changes in AR target genes such as NKX3.1 (Figure 3C) or an AR target gene signature, as discussed below (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LREX' tumors were resistant to Enz treatment.
source: In contrast to LNAR' tumors, LREX' tumors were resistant to Enz treatment, as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LREX' tumors regressed when both JQ1 +Enz were delivered in combination.
source: However, LREX' tumors regressed when both JQ1 +Enz were delivered in combination (Figure 3B), effectively re-sensitizing resistant tumors to Enz.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Some of the most potently downregulated genes in JQ1-treated LREX' tumors were GR (NR3C1) itself, the GR target gene SGK1, and MYC.
source: Of note, some of the most potently downregulated genes in JQ1-treated LREX' tumors were GR (NR3C1) itself, the GR target gene SGK1, and MYC, whereas NKX3.1 was largely unchanged (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NKX3.1 was largely unchanged in JQ1-treated LREX' tumors.
source: Of note, some of the most potently downregulated genes in JQ1-treated LREX' tumors were GR (NR3C1) itself, the GR target gene SGK1, and MYC, whereas NKX3.1 was largely unchanged (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The AR target genes NKX3.1 and TMPRSS2 were upregulated at lower JQ1 concentrations (10 nM) but moderately suppressed at higher concentrations (1 uM).
source: The AR target genes NKX3.1 and TMPRSS2 were upregulated at lower JQ1 concentrations (10 nM) but moderately suppressed at higher concentrations (1 uM) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The GR target genes SGK1 and FKBP5, as well as GR (NR3C1) itself and MYC, were consistently and more profoundly inhibited by JQ1 in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: In contrast, the GR target genes SGK1 and FKBP5, as well as GR (NR3C1) itself and MYC, were consistently and more profoundly inhibited in a dose-dependent fashion.
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Enz primarily inhibits AR-biased genes in LREX' xenografts.
source: This analysis revealed that Enz primarily inhibits AR-biased genes in LREX' xenografts, whereas JQ1 primarily inhibits GR-biased genes (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: JQ1 primarily inhibits GR-biased genes in LREX' xenografts.
source: This analysis revealed that Enz primarily inhibits AR-biased genes in LREX' xenografts, whereas JQ1 primarily inhibits GR-biased genes (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Inhibition of both AR and GR signaling pathways was observed in tumors treated with a combination of JQ1+Enz together.
source: It is not until tumors are treated with a combination of JQ1+Enz together do we see inhibition of both AR and GR signaling pathways (Figure 3E), as well as LREX' tumor regression (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3E and tumor growth data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The selective effect of JQ1 on GR but not AR in this model is likely explained by the dose-dependent sensitivity of their downstream targets coupled with challenges in achieving sustained JQ1 exposure in vivo.
source: The selective effect of JQ1 on GR but not AR in this model is likely explained by the dose-dependent sensitivity of their downstream targets (revealed in vitro) coupled with well documented challenges in achieving sustained JQ1 exposure in vivo (Matzuk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and supported by a citation.

claim: Strong bio-JQ1 binding was observed at the MYC gene locus in LNAR' and LREX' cells in the presence or absence of Enz.
source: As expected, we observed strong bio-JQ1 binding at the MYC gene locus in LNAR' and LREX' cells in the presence or absence of Enz.
evidence: This claim is supported by Chem-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BRD4 ChIP-seq showed binding of BRD4 at the MYC locus, confirming the specificity of the bio-JQ1 signal.
source: The specificity of the bio-JQ1 signal was confirmed by BRD4 ChIP-seq which showed binding of the well-known JQ1 target BRD4 at precisely the same locus (Figure 4A) as well as by the highly significant correlation of bio-JQ1 with H3K27ac (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by BRD4 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Significant bio-JQ1 binding was observed at the GR enhancer, but only in LREX' cells treated with Enz, when the H3K27ac mark is present.
source: We also observed significant bio-JQ1 binding at the GR enhancer, but only in LREX' cells treated with Enz, when the H3K27ac mark is present (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Chem-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BRD4 binding was not detected at the GR enhancer, suggesting that a different JQ1 target protein is likely responsible for driving GR expression.
source: Interestingly, we did not detect BRD4 binding at the enhancer, suggesting that a different JQ1 target protein is likely responsible for driving GR expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of BRD4 binding at the GR enhancer shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The GR enhancer is amongst the most differential bio-JQ1 binding sites, showing strong preferential binding in LREX' cells.
source: Remarkably, the GR enhancer is amongst the most differential binding sites, showing strong preferential binding in LREX' cells, whereas binding at the MYC locus is unchanged (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential peak analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Binding at the MYC locus is unchanged between LREX' and LNAR' cells.
source: Remarkably, the GR enhancer is amongst the most differential binding sites, showing strong preferential binding in LREX' cells, whereas binding at the MYC locus is unchanged (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential peak analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GR overexpression in the setting of combined JQ1+Enz rescued tumor growth.
source: Remarkably, GR overexpression in the setting of combined JQ1+Enz rescued tumor growth (Figure 4D), thereby demonstrating that the anti-tumor activity of BET inhibition in this model is mediated by GR suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The anti-tumor activity of BET inhibition in this model is mediated by GR suppression.
source: Remarkably, GR overexpression in the setting of combined JQ1+Enz rescued tumor growth (Figure 4D), thereby demonstrating that the anti-tumor activity of BET inhibition in this model is mediated by GR suppression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GR rescue experiment shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The acquisition of AR binding at the GR enhancer is likely a consequence of the reprogrammed AR cistrome in prostate cancer versus normal tissue, which is enriched at HOXB13 and FOXA1 sites.
source: We propose that the acquisition of AR binding at the enhancer, which triggers a decline in GR expression, is likely a consequence of the reprogrammed AR cistrome in prostate cancer versus normal tissue, which is enriched at HOXB13 and FOXA1 sites (Pomerantz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposal based on data and supported by a citation.

claim: Increased levels of EZH2 expression observed in CRPC may play a role in the progressive accumulation of the repressive H3K27me3 mark.
source: Increased levels of EZH2 expression observed in CRPC (Varambally et al., 2002) may play a role in the progressive accumulation of the repressive H3K27me3 mark.
evidence: This is a speculation based on data and supported by a citation.

claim: Acquired Enz resistance can occur in CRPC patients through reactivation of the normally silenced GR locus.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that acquired Enz resistance can occur in CRPC patients through reactivation of this normally silenced GR locus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Prior work has suggested that GR can attenuate AR signaling and inhibit growth in AR-positive prostate cancer models.
source: Prior work has suggested that GR can attenuate AR signaling and inhibit growth in AR-positive prostate cancer models, raising the possibility that tumor cells gain a growth advantage upon GR silencing (Yemelyanov et al., 2007; Sahu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In the setting of GR-driven Enz-resistance, where AR is still inhibited, GR can function as an activator of growth by substituting for AR.
source: However, in the setting of GR-driven Enz-resistance, where AR is still inhibited, GR can now function as an activator of growth by substituting for AR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Genes whose enhancers have high levels of H3K27ac tend to be exquisitely sensitive to BET inhibition.
source: Prior work, primarily in hematologic malignancies, showing that genes whose enhancers have high levels of H3K27ac (e.g. MYC) tend to be exquisitely sensitive to BET inhibition provides additional support to this hypothesis (Shao et al., 2014; Mertz et al., 2011; Ott et al., 2012; Delmore et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The dose of BET inhibitor required for therapeutic impact is likely to vary depending on the clinical context.
source: Regardless of the mechanism, an important implication of this differential sensitivity is that the dose of BET inhibitor required for therapeutic impact is likely to vary depending on the clinical context.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: In patients with acquired Enz resistance driven by GR, clinical benefit may be seen at lower doses of BET inhibitor than those required for AR inhibition.
source: In patients with acquired Enz resistance driven by GR, our data predicts that clinical benefit may be seen at lower doses than those required for AR inhibition.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental observations.

claim: 7 of 50 post-Enz/Abi samples had detectable AR mutations (all with AR L702H).
source: 7 of 50 post-Enz/Abi samples had detectable AR mutations (all with AR L702H, known to be activated by prednisone and enriched in post-Abi patients) with no correlation with GR levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from analysis of the SU2C dataset.

claim: AR L702H mutation is known to be activated by prednisone and enriched in post-Abi patients.
source: 7 of 50 post-Enz/Abi samples had detectable AR mutations (all with AR L702H, known to be activated by prednisone and enriched in post-Abi patients) with no correlation with GR levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: There was no correlation between AR L702H mutations and GR levels.
source: 7 of 50 post-Enz/Abi samples had detectable AR mutations (all with AR L702H, known to be activated by prednisone and enriched in post-Abi patients) with no correlation with GR levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from analysis of the SU2C dataset shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The AR-V7 splice variant was negatively correlated with GR expression (Spearman R = −0.39, p=0.03).
source: The AR-V7 splice variant was negatively correlated with GR expression (Spearman R = −0.39, p=0.03) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that GR and AR-V7 may define mutually exclusive subsets of Enz/Abi-resistant patients, although larger cohorts are needed for more definitive analysis (Antonarakis et al., 2014; Scher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct observation from statistical analysis of the SU2C dataset shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: GR and AR-V7 may define mutually exclusive subsets of Enz/Abi-resistant patients.
source: The AR-V7 splice variant was negatively correlated with GR expression (Spearman R = −0.39, p=0.03) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that GR and AR-V7 may define mutually exclusive subsets of Enz/Abi-resistant patients, although larger cohorts are needed for more definitive analysis (Antonarakis et al., 2014; Scher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the negative correlation observed, with citations to relevant studies.

claim: There was no significant increase in AR mRNA expression in the pre- versus post-Enz/Abi cases.
source: There was with no significant increase in AR mRNA expression in the pre- versus post-Enz/Abi cases (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from analysis of the SU2C dataset shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Continuous Enz exposure is required to maintain high levels of GR expression in the LNAR'/LREX' model system.
source: To explore the mechanism underlying this dynamic regulation of GR expression in prostate cancer progression, we first returned to the LNAR'/LREX' model system where continuous Enz exposure is required to maintain high levels of GR expression (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the model system shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DHT treatment suppresses GR expression in LREX cells.
source: We previously reported that dihydrotestosterone (DHT) treatment suppresses GR expression in LREX cells (Arora et al., 2013) and noted an AR binding peak that, interestingly, maps precisely to this newly defined GR enhancer, adjacent to FOXA1 and HOXB13 motifs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Enz-reversible AR binding was confirmed at the GR enhancer site in both LNAR' and LREX' cells by ChIP-PCR.
source: We confirmed Enz-reversible AR binding at this site in both LNAR' and LREX' cells by chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by polymerase-chain reaction (ChIP-PCR) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Robust Dox-inducible GR (and downstream SGK1) expression was confirmed in tumors despite JQ1 treatment.
source: To test this hypothesis, we introduced a doxycycline (Dox)-inducible allele of GR under the control of a BET-independent promoter into LREX' cells and confirmed robust Dox-inducible GR (and downstream SGK1) expression in tumors despite JQ1 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The Roadmap Epigenomics Project lacks any prostate tissue or prostate cell line data.
source: One limitation of the Roadmap Epigenomics Project is the lack of any prostate tissue or prostate cell line data.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the database.
